title: Good Article Breakdown: How Anthropic Wrote Agent Engineering into a Design Pattern Manual
subtitle: Structural Breakdown of Reading 'Building Effective Agents'
markdown: > Breakdown Target: 'Building Effective Agents', authored by Erik Schluntz and Barry Zhang, published on the Anthropic Engineering Blog on December 19, 2024. The original link is at the end of the article. This is a structural breakdown in the style of study notes; the viewpoints belong to the original article's authors. This is the most cited agent methodology article in engineering blogs. The entire article contains no new experiments and no benchmark tables; its persuasiveness comes entirely from its structure. Compared to the paper breakdowns in this series (which all sell data), this article exactly demonstrates how a methodology article without data can stand firm. ## I. Why It Is Worth Breaking Down The fate of most engineering blogs is to sink after publication, yet this article has become a citation anchor for agent engineering: the dichotomy between workflows and agents, the names of the five workflow patterns, and the term ACI are now used everywhere. It got three things right: defining first and then applying, naming patterns, and putting deterrents before teaching. All three are structural decisions, unrelated to the novelty of the method itself. The opening sentence states the stance: after collaborating with dozens of industry teams, the most successful implementations all use simple, composable patterns rather than complex frameworks. Every chapter in the article serves this sentence. ## II. The Skeleton of the Main Text: A Table of Contents with Increasing Complexity as Narrative | Chapter | Responsibility | Breakdown Key Points | | --- | --- | --- | | What are agents? | Definition first | 'agentic systems' is the umbrella term, with a dichotomy between workflows and agents | | When (and when not) to use agents | Deterrent first | Find the simplest feasible solution; add complexity only when necessary; it might not be appropriate to use an agent at all | | When and how to use frameworks | Tool perspective | The abstraction layer of frameworks comes with costs; connect directly via APIs first, and if using frameworks, understand the underlying layer | | Building blocks, workflows, and agents | Main body | Start with enhanced LLM building blocks, move to five workflow patterns, and finally to agents | | Combining and customizing | Boundary declarations | Patterns are composable and modifiable, with metrics driving iteration | | Summary | Convergence via three principles | Simplicity, transparency, and refining ACI | | Appendix 2 | Concealing the primary contribution | ACI: Mirroring the intricacies of human-computer interfaces between agents and computers | The table of contents follows an increasing order of complexity from building blocks to systems, which itself constitutes a narrative: as readers proceed sequentially, each step introduces only slightly more complexity than the previous one, arriving at agents with all prerequisite concepts already established. This structure is isomorphic to Karpathy’s training recipe article (building the skeleton first, then adding complexity item by item). ## III. Definition First: The Dichotomy Between Workflows and Agents The first section cleanly delineates terminology: 'agentic systems' is the umbrella term, divided into two categories. Workflows refer to systems where LLMs and tools are orchestrated through predefined code paths; agents refer to systems where the LLM dynamically leads its own workflow and tool usage, retaining control over how tasks are accomplished. The practical value of this dichotomy lies in decision-making: workflows trade latency and cost for performance controllability, making them suitable for tasks with clear boundaries; agents are better suited for open-ended problems where the number of steps cannot be predicted. All subsequent pattern classifications rely on this set of definitions. Establishing definitional authority first is the first structural weapon of this methodology article. ## IV. Five Workflow Patterns: In the Style of GoF Design Patterns The main body presents five workflow patterns, each written in the same format: name, one-sentence mechanism, 'When to use', and two examples. This approach directly mirrors the GoF design patterns manual, with the effect that patterns can be referenced by name: 'This requirement is adequately handled by orchestrator-workers' becomes a transmissible language within the team. | Pattern | One-sentence mechanism | Signal for applicability | | --- | --- | --- | | Prompt chaining | Tasks are decomposed into sequential steps; the output of the previous step is fed into the next, with programmatic checkpoints inserted in between | Tasks can be cleanly decomposed into fixed subtasks | | Routing | Inputs are classified first, then directed to specialized downstream prompts | Input categories are distinct, allowing separate optimization without interference | | Parallelization | Subtasks are run in parallel and then programmatically aggregated, with two variants: sectioning and voting | Subtasks are independent, or multiple perspectives are needed to increase confidence | | Orchestrator-workers | A central LLM dynamically decomposes tasks, dispatches workers, and aggregates results | The number and content of subtasks cannot be predetermined | | Evaluator-optimizer | One LLM generates, another evaluates and provides feedback, in a loop | Clear evaluation criteria exist, and iteration yields measurable benefits | The distinction between Orchestrator-workers and Parallelization best reveals one's expertise: they look similar, but the difference lies in whether subtasks are predefined. In the former, subtasks are determined by the orchestrator on the fly based on the input; in the latter, tasks are sliced first and then executed. This single sentence clearly articulates the boundary most easily confused. The Agents section concludes with a pithy quote: an agent is typically an LLM that calls tools in a loop based on environmental feedback. Each step within the loop must assess progress using ground truth from the environment (tool call results, code execution outputs), paired with a stopping condition (maximum iterations) to maintain control. Examples come from their own implementations: a coding agent for solving SWE-bench and a computer use reference implementation. ## V. Appendix 2 is the most underrated contribution of the entire article Hidden within the three principles of the Summary in the main text is a sentence: carefully refine the agent-computer interface (ACI) through thorough tool documentation and testing. Appendix 2 expands on this concept, with the core analogy being: the effort invested in the human-computer interface (HCI) by humans should be matched by equal effort invested in the interface between agents and computers. Four practical suggestions: check from the model's perspective whether tool descriptions are self-explanatory; treat parameter naming as polishing docstrings for junior engineers; run numerous examples in the sandbox to observe how the model makes mistakes; design tools with error-proofing (poka-yoke) to make errors difficult to occur. The most compelling evidence comes from their SWE-bench agent experiments: more time was spent optimizing tools than optimizing prompts. A typical case is that the model incorrectly used relative paths when outside the root directory; the issue disappeared after changing the tool parameters to enforce absolute paths. This is a concrete, convincing engineering detail that supports the concept. ## VI. Three Writing Techniques You Can Take Away 1. **Preemptive Deterrence**: Place the section on 'when not to use' in the second part. Advise against use before teaching; trust stems from restraint rather than salesmanship. 2. **Naming Convention for Modes**: Unify the four components: name, mechanism, applicable signals, and examples. This allows readers to reference your content by name. 3. **Appendix for Substantive Content**: The main body handles dissemination, while the appendix handles depth. Placing practical, hands-on content like ACI in the appendix actually increases the overall credibility and depth of the article. ## Footnote: Reflections on My Own Work The design of a post-match coaching system can directly adopt the framework presented here: The sequence of the six-step pipeline consists of predefined code paths, meaning the overall system belongs to the workflow category; only allowing an LLM to perform end-to-end free-form generation qualifies as an agent. At the current stage, we explicitly choose the former, which aligns perfectly with the principle of separating responsibilities: 'structured processing at the algorithm layer, paraphrasing at the LLM layer.' The design of structured JSON interfaces is the implementation of ACI thinking: self-explanatory field names, clear boundaries, and error prevention as a priority. Improving the verification step naturally adopts the evaluator-optimizer pattern: criteria for behavioral improvement exist prior to suggestions. ## References - Original Article: Building Effective Agents, Anthropic Engineering Blog, 2024-12-19, anthropic.com/engineering/building-effective-agents - Original Authors: Erik Schluntz, Barry Zhang (according to the original Acknowledgements) - Related Breakdowns: This blog's WebRL breakdown (using RL to teach models task decomposition, i.e., the training route from workflow to agent in the Anthropic framework); Search-R1 breakdown (loss masking belongs to error-prevention design for tool interfaces)
